public_rationale: On 2026-06-15 he wrote that any research you get from AI 'will absolutely have hallucinations.' On a plain reading, that means every AI research answer contains false or made-up content. A BBC study reported on 2025-02-11 had journalists review answers from four AI assistants to news questions. They judged that 91% of answers had at least some issue, so about 9% had no identified issue (e1). The same study found that 19% of answers citing BBC content introduced factual errors, such as wrong statements, numbers or dates (e2). A 22-broadcaster study released on 2025-10-22 found major accuracy issues, such as fabricated or outdated information, in 20% of answers (e3). That study counted only major issues, so it does not rule out minor errors in the other answers. These error rates support a warning to check AI output. But a share of whole answers had no issues identified by expert reviewers, which goes against the claim that every answer is affected.
limitations: Reviewers finding no issue in an answer does not prove the answer had no errors. Subtle errors may have been missed.
The evaluations used news questions put to general AI assistants. They did not test long or specialised 'deep research' reports, which may be more likely to contain at least one error.
The BBC figures come from a news report about the study, not the study itself. The 22-broadcaster figures come from a participant's press release.
No source gives a hallucination-specific, answer-level rate that includes minor errors for 2026 models.
If the words are read as overstatement for 'expect hallucinations', the high error rates would fit that reading better.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: every answer an AI system gives to a research or fact-finding question contains at least one hallucination, meaning false or fabricated content.

Tested with independent evaluations in which expert reviewers checked AI assistants' answers for factual errors. If a meaningful share of answers had no errors, the universal claim is contradicted. High error rates support the speaker's broader warning but not the universal 'any... absolutely'.

No period was given. The claim is read as describing the AI assistants in public use from 2024 up to the post date (2026-06-15). The checking requirement applies to each whole answer, not to single sentences.
criteria.support_condition: Credible evaluations finding that all, or essentially all, AI research answers contain at least one false or fabricated claim.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evaluations finding that a meaningful share of AI answers to research questions contain no factual errors or issues.
